q-253547.problem:
Consider the set $B,$ defined as

$$
B=\{\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+1}:n\in \{0,1,2,3,4\}\}.
$$

What is the infimum of $B?$

q-253547.worked_solution:
The infimum of a set $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B.$

If $B$ is a finite set, the infimum of $B$ equals its minimum.

First, let's write down all the terms of our set by substituting $n=0,1,2,3,4$ into the expression for the elements of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(0)^{2}+1} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{(1)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{(2)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{1}{(3)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{(4)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{17}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
B=\{1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}inf(B) & =min\{1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}=\frac{1}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

inf(B)=max(-\infty ,\pi ]=\pi .

q-253134.name: Question 5
q-253134.problem:
Consider the following set.

$$
A=\{(-1)^{n}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}}\,:\,n\in N\}
$$

For this set, we have that {{field-1}}.
q-253134.worked_solution:
The supremum of $A$ is the smallest upper bound of $A.$

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=(-1)^{n}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166808/assets/690c0466ffac72597e9378539d1540d6baaa49c7cbe77bee8cc83ab00f065635.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is an oscillating sequence converging to $0.$ The maximum of $A$ is 

$$
max(A)={a}_{2}=(-1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2+1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\ge {a}_{2}$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $x<{a}_{2}$ cannot be an upper bound because ${a}_{2},$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $x.$

Therefore, $[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
sup(A)=min[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\infty )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

Notice that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ is the maximum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

$$
sup(A)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\in A.
$$

EXPLANATION

The supremum of A is the smallest upper bound of A.

To find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing all upper bounds of A (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

The elements of A are the terms of the sequence an, given by an=(−1)n⋅1n+1,n∈N={1,2,3,4,…}.

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

We see that an is an oscillating sequence converging to 0. The maximum of A is max(A)=a2=(−1)2⋅12+1=13.

So, in our case, we have that

  • any number x≥a2 is an upper bound of A,

  • any number x<a2 cannot be an upper bound because a2, an element of A, is greater than x.

Therefore, [13,∞) is the set of upper bounds of A, and

sup(A)=min[13,∞)=13. Notice that 13 is the maximum of A. Therefore, we conclude that

sup(A)=13∈A.

q-253138.problem:

$$

q-253138.worked_solution:
The infimum of $A$ is the greatest lower bound of $A.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=n\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ),\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166808/assets/bcece2e5bdef3c9d939d953fbeb0c5163d9343004cd309f28db37bf9b5b089ef.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is an oscillating, non-convergent sequence. Moreover, $A$ is unbounded below. In other words, we can always find a sufficiently large $n$ so that ${a}_{n}$ is smaller than $x$ for any real number $x.$ Therefore, $A$ has no lower bounds and $inf(A)\,=-\infty .$

The elements of A are the terms of the sequence an, given by

What is the supremum of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?

${sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=$
{{field-1}}
q-253869.worked_solution:
The supremum of a function is the supremum of the range of the function.

In this case, the range of $f$ is $A=(-1,4].$

To find the supremum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $y\ge 4$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $y<4$ cannot be an upper bound of $A$ because $4,$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $y.$

Therefore, $[4,\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and

$$
{sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=sup(A)=min[4,\infty )=4.
$$
